14.0.0.en: The Greeks: those who attend the synagogue of the Jews and heard the two Apostles and believed in Christ.

14.0.1.en: Made their minds evil affected: they stirred them up against the two Apostles and their teachings, saying that they oppose their religion and cause disorder in the city.

14.0.2.en: The Gentiles: the pagan Greeks in the city who do not attend the synagogue of the Jews and hold fast to their paganism; and for the sake of evil the wicked Jews united with the pagans in hostility to the two Apostles so as to be a force to resist the preaching of Christ.

14.0.3.en: The brethren: the Christians who believed, whether from the Jews or the Greeks. The Jews who rejected the faith were greatly troubled that Jews like themselves had believed in Christ, and they call the Greeks who believed in Christ brethren, because by this they feel that they have lost their distinction as the chosen people of God, since they used to despise the Gentiles. In the city of Iconium the preaching began in the synagogue of the Jews as usual, and many Jews and proselytes believed, which stirred up those of the Jews who did not believe, so they began to deceive the Gentiles with corrupt words and to push them to oppose those who had believed.

14.1.0.en: Abode they long time speaking boldly: the two Apostles were not afraid of the opposition of the Jews who rejected faith in Christ, and continued preaching to the Jews and the Gentiles with courage.

14.1.1.en: Gave testimony unto the word of his grace by: 1- the convincing proofs in the words of the two Apostles.

14.1.2.en: 2- the joining of many to the faith.

14.1.3.en: 3- the working of various miracles such as healing the sick and casting out demons.

14.1.4.en: Signs and wonders to be done by their hands: miracles to confirm the faith of those who believed and to draw others to faith, and trust in the word of God on the lips of the two Apostles.

14.2.0.en: A division occurred among the people of the city, as some of them were on the side of the Jews and others on the side of the two Apostles.

14.3.0.en: Both of the Gentiles, and also of the Jews with their rulers: the unbelieving Jews united with the Gentiles who held fast to their paganism, under the leadership of the rulers of the Jews and the rulers of the Gentiles.

14.3.1.en: An assault: the planning of a plot to attack and arrest the two Apostles.

14.3.2.en: To use them despitefully: to wrong them and accuse them of being wicked, saying that they had stirred up the city and were preaching wrong ideas, namely their claim that Jesus is God.

14.3.3.en: To stone them: their intention was to sentence them to death by stoning.

14.4.0.en: They were ware of it, and fled: not out of fear, but to continue preaching and winning souls for Christ.

14.4.1.en: Lycaonia: a province or district in Asia Minor, that is, present-day Turkey.

14.4.2.en: Lystra: a large city in the south of Lycaonia about 40 miles from Iconium.

14.4.3.en: Derbe: a large city in Lycaonia about 25 miles from Lystra.

14.4.4.en: The region that lieth round about: it is clear that the two Apostles, on their journey to Lystra and from it to Derbe, preached in the lands through which they passed.

14.4.5.en: It is beautiful for a person not to be hindered by negatives but always to strive for what is positive. If a door is closed before you, do not be troubled, but look for the open door and continue in your service and faithfulness in your work and love for those around you.

14.5.0.en: Never had walked: this shows his permanent disability for many years, and that there was no medical treatment that would benefit him.

14.5.1.en: In the city of Lystra there was a man who had been lame from his birth.

14.6.0.en: The same heard Paul speak: it seems that they used to put this lame man in one of the marketplaces, so Paul took this place, where many gather, to preach in it; and this lame man, who sat there to beg, paid attention to Paul’s preaching and listened to him.

14.6.1.en: Perceiving that he had faith: signs of conviction by Paul’s words appeared on his face, in addition to the gift of the Holy Spirit in the sacrament of the priesthood, which helped Paul to understand and know his readiness and faith.

14.7.0.en: With a loud voice: this shows Paul’s authority in healing, and to alert all those present to the miracle so that they would believe.

14.7.1.en: Leaped: jumped, and this shows that he received strength in his muscles that enabled him not only to walk but also to jump, and this shows the power of the miracle.

14.7.2.en: Paul called the lame man to stand on his feet, and he leaped and was healed immediately.

14.8.0.en: What Paul had done: he commanded the lame man, with authority, to stand, and he stood at once.

14.8.1.en: Lifted up their voices: they cried out in a loud voice and glorified the gods.

14.8.2.en: In the speech of Lycaonia: their local language; and at the same time they knew the Greek language in which Paul was preaching because it is the language spread throughout the whole world, but when a person is excited he speaks spontaneously in his original language however well he knows the foreign language.

14.8.3.en: The crowds of hearers were dazzled and spoke in the local language, which the two Apostles did not understand, and this confirms that the Holy Spirit had not given them the gift of speaking in tongues or interpretation in this situation, because they were speaking in the Greek language; and they said that Paul and Barnabas were the gods Hermes and Zeus. Hermes was the Greek god of eloquence and his symbol was the planet Mercury, and Zeus was the god of the gods and his symbol was Jupiter, and they believed that Hermes was the interpreter and the spokesman for Zeus, so they thought that Paul was Hermes because he preaches and speaks more than Barnabas, and Barnabas was Zeus, the god of the gods and the foremost of all the gods.

14.9.0.en: Before their city: where a statue or temple of the gods stands.

14.9.1.en: The gates: the gates of the city near the temple of the gods.

14.9.2.en: The people: this shows that the people of the city were all, or at least mostly, pagans. The priest of Zeus came with oxen, which are the greatest of the sacrifices, and garlands, which are used in the worship of idols, to offer them to the two Apostles.

14.10.0.en: Heard of: at first the two Apostles did not understand the speech of the crowd because it was in a language strange to them, but when they saw the crowds moving toward the gates of the city and preparing the oxen and the garlands, they asked what was happening, and they told them of their belief that they were the gods Zeus and Hermes and that they wanted to offer them the worship and honor that befit them.

14.10.1.en: Rent their clothes: a Jewish custom, also found among some peoples, as in Upper Egypt, as an expression of great grief or distress.

14.10.2.en: Crying out: they had to cry out because the crowd was speaking and even shouting, so they were forced to cry out so that they would hear them.

14.11.0.en: Why do ye these things: they rebuke them for trying to offer worship to them.

14.11.1.en: Of like passions with you: exposed to hunger, thirst and sickness, and therefore we are not gods, because gods are not exposed to the troubles of men, as the pagans believe.

14.11.3.en: The living God: not like the lifeless idols that neither speak nor move.

14.11.4.en: The two Apostles declared to the crowds that they were men like them, and that they were preaching to them the worship of the one God the Creator and not these many vain gods.

14.12.0.en: In times past: from the beginning of creation to the Incarnation of Christ.

14.12.1.en: Suffered: He was longsuffering toward the peoples of the world.

14.12.2.en: Their own ways: the mistaken pagan worship, from which they did not turn back even though it wearied them greatly. God left the Gentiles, from the creation of the world to the coming of Christ, to walk in their own ways, and chose only the Jews as a people for Himself.

14.13.0.en: He left not himself without witness: God declares Himself to the Jews through His speaking with the prophets, but He shows Himself to the whole world through the conscience, which is the voice of God within every person, and through His good gifts that He bestows on the whole world, for they all testify to His existence and His love.

14.13.1.en: Rain: it waters man, animals and plants, so the deserts are built up and God’s love appears. Fruitful seasons: weather conditions that help the plants to grow, so they give fruit that man and animals eat.

14.13.2.en: Food and gladness: when a person finds his food, he rejoices and enjoys it, and he should then thank God, who gave him his material needs and gladdened his heart.

14.14.0.en: With these sayings: by their declaring that they were men and that God is far higher than they supposed and that He is the doer of good to mankind.

14.14.1.en: The two Apostles were able, with difficulty, to keep the crowds from offering sacrifices to them.

14.15.0.en: Jews from Antioch and Iconium: those who rejected faith in Christ and drove Paul and Barnabas out of their cities.

14.15.1.en: Persuaded the people: that Paul and Barnabas speak wrong teachings and curse the gods because they said that their worship is vain, and even claim that a man called Jesus is God; and perhaps they attributed the miracle of raising the lame man to the Apostles’ relationship with Beelzebub, as they had accused Christ before.

14.15.2.en: Stoned Paul: they struck him with stones until he fell to the ground wounded and unconscious.

14.15.3.en: Drew him out of the city: so that the wild beasts would eat his corpse, as contempt and abuse of him.

14.15.4.en: Jews arrived from Antioch of Pisidia and Iconium and stirred up the crowds, and they stoned Paul and dragged him outside the city after they thought he was dead, so that he would not be buried in the city and become famous by his body as a great teacher.

14.16.0.en: The disciples: those from Lystra who believed and became disciples of Christ.

14.16.1.en: Rose up: it seems he was unconscious from the violence of the stoning and then recovered, and perhaps God gave him strength and healing so that he was able to stand and walk.

14.16.2.en: The next day: the very next day, so the wicked who thought they had killed him did not notice him, and he left Lystra quickly because there was no opportunity for service in it at that time, and headed to a new place to preach in it. Barnabas: it is evident from the foregoing that Barnabas was not harmed because of his silence, whereas Paul, because of his much defending and preaching, was exposed to death.

14.16.3.en: When the Christians surrounded Paul they found him alive, so he rose and came with Barnabas to Derbe. We note that Paul faced the stoning which he used to be glad to carry out against the Christians, such as Stephen, to whose stoning he was a witness before he believed.

14.16.4.en: The opinions of people are changeable, so do not cling to them; for after they honored the two Apostles they rose against them to kill them. Care about God’s opinion of you even if people object, and do not please others at God’s expense, but hold fast to His word however great the pressures on you.

14.17.s.en: (3) In Derbe, then the return to Antioch

14.17.0.en: That city: it is Derbe, and those who opposed him in Lystra did not follow him.

14.17.1.en: Taught many: no opposition to the ministry is mentioned in this city, so many believed and became disciples of Christ.

14.17.2.en: They returned again to Lystra, and to Iconium, and Antioch: the courage of Paul and Barnabas appears in their returning to the lands from which they had been driven out and where they had even been plotted against to be killed; but most likely they did not preach openly among the crowds, but met with the believers and confirmed them in the faith.

14.17.3.en: The two Apostles began the preaching in Derbe, and many believed, then they returned to Lystra, Iconium and Antioch.

14.18.0.en: Confirming: they encourage the believers because of the great harassment from the wicked around them. Through much tribulation: it is a proof of man’s love for God and his holding fast to Him and his not clinging to the world. The kingdom of God: the heavenly Kingdom.

14.18.1.en: The two Apostles went on confirming the faith of the disciples and making clear to them the importance of enduring tribulations to receive salvation.

14.19.0.en: Had prayed with fasting: this shows the importance of fasting and prayer in choosing priests and preparing them for service. The two Apostles did not choose priests when they began preaching in these cities, either because they were driven out and had no time to ordain priests, or they may have postponed the ordination of priests until the Church grew, even a little, and someone appeared in it who was worthy of this rank in terms of his spiritual readiness and his bearing the responsibility of service. Commended them: they regarded these churches as a deposit which they placed in the hand of God, in whom they trusted that He would keep them and make them grow.

14.19.1.en: The two Apostles appointed priests (the word means, from the Syriac qashishu, elders), and the people used to elect them and then the Apostles would sign them with the cross; and they organized the ministry in the churches, and prayed and fasted with them, then left them in the care of God.

14.20.0.en: Pisidia: after they had confirmed the believers in Antioch, the capital of Pisidia, they passed through the province of Pisidia, and perhaps they preached in some of these lands.

14.20.1.en: Pamphylia: a province in Asia Minor next to Pisidia.

14.20.2.en: Preached the word in Perga: it seems that they did not preach in Perga, a large city in the province of Pamphylia, when they visited it the previous time (ch. 13:13), but now they preached Christ in it. Attalia: a port in Asia Minor to which the two Apostles went in order to sail from it to Syrian Antioch. The two Apostles passed through Pisidia to Pamphylia and preached in Perga, then came to the port of Attalia.

14.21.0.en: Recommended: the Church had sent them for preaching and committed them into the hand of God, who blessed their journey and made it successful.

14.21.1.en: The work which they fulfilled: the preaching in the cities through which they passed during their journey.

14.21.2.en: The two Apostles sailed back to Antioch of Syria, where they had begun their journey, by the grace of God.

14.22.0.en: When they arrived at Antioch, they gathered the believers and told them of God’s work with them on the journey, and that God had called many of the Gentiles to faith.

14.23.0.en: After the first journey, which took about three years and began in A.D. 45, they stayed two years in Antioch with the believers as they had been before the journey; that is, they served two years in the Church of Antioch in Syria.

14.23.1.en: When a person finds that he has completed what the Lord asked of him, he is made very happy and thanks God for what He accomplished for him and through him. So, my brother, be careful to complete every service and responsibility given to you, because it is from God and you will give account for it before Him, and then He will help you and gladden your heart.

14.23.2.en: The Council of Jerusalem and the beginning of the second journey

15.0.0.en: From Judea: where Jerusalem is the center of Jewish worship, so those who believed in Christ there feel responsible for caring for the rest of the churches in the world because Christ was crucified in Jerusalem, and because they still held fast to the Law of Moses that they had lived by all their lives and were unable to perceive that it was a symbol and a preparation for Christianity.

15.0.1.en: Some Christians of Jewish origin came, who had not been convinced by the vision of Peter and the Baptism of Cornelius, and who afterward became roots of the Ebionite heresy that appeared at the end of the first century and from which the Adventists or Sabbatarians are now descended; these came from Jerusalem to Antioch teaching the Christians of Gentile origin that they must be circumcised and keep all the Jewish rituals in order to receive salvation.

15.1.0.en: Dissension and disputation: the discussion became heated between Paul and Barnabas on the one hand and the Christians of Jewish origin who came from Judea on the other, and they did not reach any agreement. They determined: those gathered from both parties agreed to return to the leadership of the Church represented in the Apostles, who made Jerusalem their center and go out from it to preach and then return to it. This is what is mentioned in (Gal 2:1-9) that Paul went up to Jerusalem by a divine revelation, that is, that God commanded him to go to Jerusalem to obtain a decision from the council of the Apostles in this matter, and those gathered agreed to that. Certain other of them: delegates from the Church of Antioch.

15.1.1.en: The elders: the priests, that is, the priests who assisted the Apostles. Here it appears that the leadership of the Church is the council of the Apostles and priests, which is now the council of bishops called the Holy Synod.

15.1.2.en: Paul and Barnabas strongly opposed those who came from Judea, then they arranged that they should go up with some Christians of Antioch to the Apostles and the priests in Jerusalem to examine this matter.

15.2.0.en: Great joy: the Christians in Lebanon (Phenicia) and the northern part of the land of the Jews (Samaria) were not fanatical for the Law of Moses, because they had long been lax in holding to it, so they rejoiced at the faith of the Gentiles without their becoming Jews.

15.2.1.en: Paul and Barnabas went out, officially sent by the Church of Antioch to Jerusalem, and passed through Phenicia and Samaria, and told of the faith of the Gentiles and their joining the Church, and the believers rejoiced at that.

15.3.0.en: The two Apostles and those with them arrived at Jerusalem, and its Church welcomed them as an official delegation from the Church of Antioch, and they told everyone the news of the first journey and how many of the Gentiles believed, were baptized and became Christians; and this news came before the convening of the council and as a preparation for it.

15.4.0.en: Many came who had been Pharisees originally, that is, holding fast to the Law of Moses, and they began to oppose the words of Paul and those with him about the faith of the Gentiles, and proclaimed the importance of circumcision and the Law for the believers of Gentile origin to be saved.

15.4.1.en: Here we see the breadth of heart of the Church, for it does not reject an opinion except after discussion and prayer and conviction of what is right and without arbitrariness, and this is the sound method in leading the Church so that everyone is convinced and a chance is given to the heretics to repent.

15.4.2.en: May you apply this in your home so that you win all the members of your family, and respect the opinions of your children even if they are small, and convince them of what is right with longsuffering.

15.5.0.en: The apostles and elders: whether those in Jerusalem or those who came from the neighboring lands of Judea, and by this they formed the first council in the history of the Church in A.D. 50.

15.5.1.en: A council of the Apostles and priests was convened, and many discussions took place among them about whether circumcision and the Law are necessary for the believers or not.

15.6.0.en: Much disputing: at the beginning of the council, the discussion continued for a long time between Paul and those with him and the Christians of Jewish origin, on the importance of circumcision and the Law for salvation. A good while ago: about 10 years ago, when Cornelius was preached to in Caesarea.

15.6.1.en: Peter rose to present his point of view, since he was the first to preach to the Gentiles by divine revelation when he preached to Cornelius and those with him.

15.7.0.en: Which knoweth the hearts: He who knows the readiness of the hearts of men for faith.

15.7.1.en: Bare them witness: by the preaching of Peter.

15.7.2.en: Giving them the Holy Ghost: whose gifts appeared in their speaking in tongues, so they received the same power of the Holy Spirit that the Christians of Jewish origin received.

15.7.3.en: Peter explained how the Holy Spirit descended on the Gentiles before they were baptized, to show God’s approval of their Baptism without circumcision or keeping the commandments of the Law.

15.8.0.en: The faith of the Gentiles in Christ has purified their hearts, with no difference between them and the believers from the Jews.

15.9.0.en: Tempt ye God: we set conditions for salvation that God did not set, for He required faith, Baptism and life in the Church, and did not ask Christians for circumcision and the Law. If God has accepted the Gentiles, how can we ask them for a proof of their faith, namely circumcision and keeping the Law? By this we are tempting God, especially since the Jews were unable to keep the whole Law, so how can we demand it of the Gentiles.

15.10.0.en: The grace of the Lord Jesus: which gives faith and the Holy Sacraments. We shall be saved: we Christians of Jewish origin.

15.10.1.en: Even as they: the Christians of Gentile origin.

15.10.2.en: The grace of God is what saves everyone through faith.

15.11.0.en: The hearers kept silent, as a sign of their agreement, and Paul and Barnabas began to describe the miracles that had been done among the Gentiles through them on their journey.

15.11.1.en: Encourage those far from God to join the Church, showing God’s love for all, especially sinners. Do not demand many things of them, and give an opportunity for their love to move first toward God.

15.12.0.en: James: he is James the son of Alphaeus, one of the twelve Apostles, the son of the maternal aunt of Christ and the bishop of Jerusalem, the writer of the Epistle of James, called the Just, and he is the president of the Council of Jerusalem. St. James spoke and asked everyone to listen.

15.13.0.en: The Apostle James made clear that God had accepted the Gentiles into the faith at the hand of Peter when he baptized Cornelius and those with him, then confirmed His acceptance of them at the hand of Paul and Barnabas when they preached and founded churches among the Gentiles.

15.14.0.en: After this: after the Jewish worship deviated into preoccupation with the letter and not the spirit, and indeed the Jews were neglectful and busied themselves with their desires, so the Jewish nation was exposed to captivity and the destruction of the Temple. The tabernacle of David, which is fallen down: he means the Tabernacle of Meeting, that is, the Jewish worship that deviated and fell in the sight of God.

15.14.1.en: I will build again the ruins thereof: this worship was destroyed, but God restores it and completes it through Christian worship. The residue of men: those other than the Jews who live around them.

15.14.2.en: The Gentiles, upon whom my name is called: all human beings are created in the image and likeness of God, and they are the children of God, and He calls them in the fullness of time to faith in Christ.

15.14.3.en: Who doeth all these things: He who created mankind and chose the Jews as a people particular to Himself, then became incarnate and accomplished redemption and receives the Jews and the Gentiles into faith in Christ.

15.14.4.en: Known unto God: all the foregoing is in God’s plan from eternity, to redeem all mankind and receive them into faith in Him.

15.14.5.en: James declared that the acceptance of the Gentiles was prophesied by the prophets, as in (Amos 9:12, 11), that God will rebuild the Jewish Church that went astray, and then will receive the Gentiles also, because God is for all and calls all, for He is their Creator, and this is His eternal plan.

15.15.0.en: Trouble: the Christians of Gentile origin are being required to fulfill the Law of Moses in order to be saved.

15.15.1.en: Which are turned to God: those who leave the worship of idols to believe in Christ.

15.15.2.en: James declared that his opinion is not to require circumcision and the Law of the Christians of Gentile origin.

15.16.0.en: Blood: the Law of Moses forbade the drinking of blood (Deut 12:16), and so does Christianity, because blood represents the life of a person, so whoever drinks blood is as if he sheds the blood of another and treats his life lightly, and this actually used to happen when a man killed another and drank of his blood in revenge on him, and still today we find one threatening another with the words (I will drink of your blood). James was content to require the Christians of Gentile origin to abstain from taking part in the feasts of the unclean idols and from practicing fornication, which was a part of idol worship, and from eating strangled animals because their blood is still in them, and likewise from drinking blood, both of which are among the prohibitions of the Law.

15.17.0.en: Moses: he means the five books of Moses, which forbid fornication and the drinking of blood.

15.17.1.en: Of old time: for hundreds of years.

15.17.2.en: In every city: the cities to which the Jews emigrated, and likewise in the cities of Judea, they established synagogues in which the Holy Scriptures are read.

15.17.3.en: Every sabbath day: the day of rest that is set apart for worship and attending the synagogues.

15.17.4.en: It is known in the whole world through the synagogues of the Jews that the Law forbids eating what is strangled and blood, so the Christians of Gentile origin must be committed to not eating or drinking blood and likewise to not committing fornication, like their brethren of Jewish origin, for this is necessary for all Christians, because blood stirs up desire and fornication is a grave sin.

15.17.5.en: Keep away from mixing with the wicked lest you share in their sins, and open your heart in love to everyone in general relations, praying for them and committed to good conduct, and you will be an example for all.

15.18.s.en: (4) Communicating the decisions of the council

15.18.0.en: Chief men among the brethren: to confirm the decisions of the council, for they were not content to send a letter lest some doubt that it was forged by Paul and Barnabas.

15.18.1.en: Barsabas: that is, son of Saba.

15.18.2.en: Silas: who is also called Silvanus.

15.18.3.en: The Apostles and the priests and the whole Council of Jerusalem decided to send delegates with Paul and Barnabas to Antioch to represent the Church of Jerusalem, and they were Judas surnamed Barsabas and Silas, who became the companion of the Apostle Paul on his second journey, and they were well-known believers.

15.19.0.en: The council gave the delegates sent to the churches of Syria and Turkey a letter carrying the decisions of the council, and began it by sending greeting.

15.20.0.en: Subverting your souls: they cast doubt on the believers and caused disturbance in their souls.

15.20.1.en: The council made clear that the Christians of Jewish origin who went from Jerusalem to Antioch and proclaimed the necessity of circumcision and keeping the Law for believers of Gentile origin, these were not sent by the Church in Jerusalem.

15.21.0.en: Being assembled with one accord: after dialogue and differences of opinion, they agreed on one opinion.

15.21.1.en: Our beloved: to show the degree of the Apostles’ trust in and love for Paul and Barnabas, and therefore in their teaching. The opinion of all agreed to send two men with Barnabas and Paul, whom the Apostles describe as having risked death for the preaching of Christ, and they would tell them the decision of the council orally also.

15.22.0.en: Things offered to idols: not only the meats, but all the corruptions connected with these feasts.

15.22.1.en: Ye shall do well: the sound conduct that is commended before God.

15.22.2.en: James declared the decision of the council, which resulted from the meeting of the Holy Spirit and the Apostles and the priests, the leaders of the Church, showing that God is the One who leads the Church through prayer and guides it in all its affairs. The decision was not to require of them anything except abstaining from eating what is sacrificed to idols, from drinking blood, from eating what is strangled, and from fornication.

15.23.0.en: The delegates arrived with the message of the council at Antioch, so they gathered the members of the Church and delivered the letter to them.

15.24.0.en: When the letter was read, the believers rejoiced and were comforted by it, as they became sure that their faith was sound and that they did not need circumcision and the Law, and the dispute and clash in the Church ended and the barrier between the Christians of Jewish and Gentile origin was removed, and they saw the support and joy of the Mother Church in Jerusalem in them, and this was an encouragement to the spread of the Church among the Gentiles in the whole world.

15.25.0.en: Prophets also themselves: prophecy in the New Testament means telling of the future, which is the Kingdom of Heaven, that is, preaching and teaching preparation for eternal life.

15.25.1.en: Judas and Silas began to preach to the people in Antioch and to encourage them in the spiritual life and confirm them in the faith.

15.26.0.en: After Judas and Silas completed their mission in Antioch, the Church sent them off in peace to return to the Apostles in Jerusalem.

15.27.0.en: It seems that some of the believers held on to Silas so that he would stay with them, so he did not return with Judas to Jerusalem and continued serving in the Church of Antioch.

15.28.0.en: Paul and Barnabas continued to complete their ministry in the Church of Antioch which they had begun before going to Jerusalem and its council, and with them were many servants who preached in Antioch and the lands around it.

15.28.1.en: The one Holy Spirit leads the Church through its bishops and priests. May you be committed to the mind of the Church and not to your personal opinions, and if you are perplexed about something, return to the Fathers of the Church and its servants so that you may live by the one Spirit and devote yourself to growing in the love of God.

15.29.s.en: (5) The beginning of the second journey

15.29.0.en: Some days after: it is thought to be about a year that Paul and Barnabas spent in the service of the Church of Antioch after the Council of Jerusalem, that is, they began the second journey about A.D. 51.

15.29.1.en: After about a year, Paul suggested to Barnabas that they make a second journey to visit those whom they had preached to on the first journey, and to check on their condition. This points to the importance of visitation in following up the effect of the word of God.

15.30.0.en: Barnabas thought that they should take Mark, the son of his sister, with them on the second preaching journey as on the first.

15.31.0.en: Paul did not agree, because Mark had not completed the first journey with them, but returned from the province of Pamphylia to Jerusalem.

15.32.0.en: As a result of the difference between Paul and Barnabas (which was without hatred or ill will, since Paul commended Barnabas in (1 Cor 9:6), and commended Mark in (2 Tim 4:11 and Col 4:10-11), each of them went to preach with another companion. Thus two teams were formed for preaching instead of one team, and Barnabas traveled with Mark to visit Cyprus, the original homeland of Barnabas, and there they preached until Barnabas was killed by being beaten with sticks.

15.33.0.en: Recommended by the brethren unto the grace of God: they bade him farewell with prayers, that God might keep him during his preaching journey.

15.33.1.en: Paul went with Silas to serve in Syria and Turkey (Cilicia).

15.33.2.en: If a difference of opinion occurs with those around you, do not lose your peace, and take care that the result is a positive one with which God is pleased even if it differs from your thinking and planning, for God turns everything to good for those who love Him.

15.33.3.en: The second journey and Paul’s preaching in Europe and Asia
